name: Refeed days / diet breaks

lead: Refeed days and diet breaks are planned periods of increased food intake, often extra carbohydrate, inserted into a calorie-restricted diet. People who diet for a lean look use them in the belief that they aid adherence, training and fullness of the muscles.
Because carbohydrate is stored with water, a refeed can raise scale weight and change how full or flat the physique looks.

paras: Proponents attribute benefits to restoring glycogen and moderating hunger and hormonal responses to dieting. Glycogen is stored with roughly three to four parts water, which accounts for short-term weight changes.
Documented risks are mainly practical, such as stalling the calorie deficit or triggering overeating. People with eating disorders are generally advised against rigid diet cycles.

lead: Refeed days and diet breaks are planned periods of higher energy intake, commonly of extra carbohydrate, within a longer calorie-restricted diet. A refeed usually lasts a day or two, while a diet break lasts longer, such as a week at maintenance intake. They are discussed in bodybuilding and appearance-focused dieting communities.

Proponents say they help dieters stick to a plan, support training and counter hunger. The wiki's reference material for this entry is limited, and no clinical study on appearance outcomes was located. One physiological detail that is documented is that glycogen is stored with water, so carbohydrate intake changes can shift scale weight in the short term [1].
infobox: Planned higher-calorie days or weeks within a diet

paras: Refeeds raise calorie intake, usually through carbohydrate, for short periods, while diet breaks pause the deficit for longer. They are related to carbohydrate loading and carb cycling, in which carbohydrate intake is deliberately varied [2].

Glycogen is stored hydrated with about three to four parts water per part glycogen [1], so a carbohydrate-rich refeed can restore glycogen and add water weight. Carbohydrate loading in endurance sport is documented to cause water retention and weight gain of this kind [2]. Proponents also describe psychological and hormonal rationales, which are not substantiated by the sources reviewed here.

No studies found in the sources reviewed for this entry. Related research includes work on intermittent energy restriction, which reviews describe as producing weight loss comparable to continuous calorie restriction, with limited evidence overall [3].

lore.intro: Refeeds and diet breaks are discussed in cutting and physique threads as tools for staying lean while keeping energy up.

claims.claim: Refeeds make the physique look fuller.
Refeeds restart fat loss or prevent metabolic slowdown.
